label: Parallel Normal Fields
notes: Open by placing the chapter in the curve part of the course. The source span is printed pages 47 through 57, and the assigned notebook turns those ideas into checks and visuals. The lecture question is how to store the bending of a space curve in a fixed normal plane without carrying along arbitrary twist.

label: From Acceleration To Normal-Plane Data
notes: Frame the whole lecture as a data compression problem. For a unit speed curve, the tangent already records speed, while its derivative points normally and records bending. The difficulty is that the normal plane moves with the curve, so a curvature signal cannot be compared at two parameter values until the normal planes have been identified.

label: Normal Fields And Parallelness
notes: Spend time on the derivative split. A normal field can change length, can rotate inside the normal plane, or can merely slide because the tangent direction changes. Parallel normal fields are the third behavior only: their derivative has no normal-plane component, so they avoid adding artificial twist to the curve.

label: Parallel Transport Is An Orthogonal Map
notes: Present the existence theorem as an initial value problem rather than as a mystical transport rule. Choose one normal vector at the initial point, solve the linear ODE, and get a unique normal field. Applying the same construction to a basis preserves all inner products, so the normal planes are identified by an orthogonal map.

label: Parallel Curves: Offset Without Twisting
notes: Use the offset curve as the geometric payoff of parallel transport. If a parallel normal field has small enough constant length, adding it to the curve produces a nearby curve with no extra spin around the tangent. The displayed inequality is a practical guardrail: the offset radius must be smaller than the local radius of curvature.

label: Hasimoto Curvature
notes: Now pull the acceleration back to the initial normal plane. The tangent derivative is a vector in the moving normal plane, and parallel transport lets us encode it as a single curve Psi in the fixed normal space at the starting point. The minus sign is convention; the conceptual move is the fixed-plane encoding.

label: Curvature Function And Gauge
notes: Once the initial normal plane has an oriented orthonormal basis, Psi becomes a coordinate vector kappa. This is the space-curve analogue of signed curvature for plane curves. The important caveat is gauge freedom: a different positive basis rotates all coordinates by one fixed special orthogonal matrix.

label: Reconstruction ODE
notes: This slide is the constructive theorem. Given kappa, an initial point, and an initial tangent, solve the frame equations and then integrate the tangent. Orthogonality is not an extra assumption after the solve; it is preserved by the skew-coupled system, which is why the reconstructed curve stays unit speed.

label: Calculus In Normal Coordinates
notes: Explain why the curvature function is useful beyond reconstruction. Every normal field can be written in the transported basis as N y. Differentiating separates a tangential term, controlled by the inner product of kappa and y, from the normal derivative N y prime. This turns moving-frame calculus into fixed-coordinate bookkeeping.

label: Elasticity Becomes A Vector ODE
notes: Connect back to the variational material from earlier chapters. For torsion-free elastic curves, the Euler-Lagrange condition becomes a second order equation for the curvature vector. In the plane this is a scalar equation; in higher codimension it is the same equation with the curvature vector moving in the normal data plane.

label: Reading Shape From Kappa
notes: Use the classification table as a geometric dictionary. Zero kappa means the tangent never changes, a nonzero constant signal gives a circle, and linear constraints on the image of kappa force the curve into a hyperplane or sphere. The learner should read the curvature trace first and predict the ambient shape before seeing the curve.

label: Diagnostics And Takeaways
notes: Close by tying the lecture to the notebook checks. Parallel transport should keep the frame orthonormal, keep transported normals perpendicular to the tangent, preserve orientation determinant, and reconstruct curves up to a rigid motion. Those checks are not optional decoration; they are the way computational geometry earns trust in this chapter.
